01  /  The Challenge

The Brief

Checkatrade had a clear ambition. They wanted to reach a generation of younger, first time homeowners who were not yet part of their world. This was an audience that was coming to home ownership for the first time, discovering what it meant to look after a property, and beginning to build the habits and brand loyalties that would stay with them for years.

To reach them, Checkatrade needed to show up differently. They wanted content that put entertainment genuinely first. Something that did not feel like an advert, that felt authentic to how that audience actually consumes content, and that would help change how a new generation thought and felt about the brand.

With only just over 2,000 YouTube subscribers, they set their target of 30,000 engagements in a month.

02  /  The Concept

The Idea

What happens when you give three celebrities with no DIY know how all the literal tools they need to succeed?

They can command a red carpet but cannot hang a shelf and would not know a spirit level from a spatula. Now they are rolling up their sleeves and joining forces with the real heroes of home improvement, a proper Checkatrade approved tradesperson, to finally learn the skills they have been avoiding their whole lives.

Across three episodes, each celebrity spends a day on the tools alongside professional carpenter Rob Bent. They learn real skills, tackle a real job, and help a deserving family get the home improvements they desperately need, completely for free.

The whole format was built around one commitment: setting each celebrity up for success. They were all, by their own admission, genuinely useless with tools at the start of the day. By the end, every one of them had built something real for a family that needed it. Every reveal landed. And at a point during each episode, when Rob stepped back and left them to complete a task on their own, every single one of them could actually do it.

That is also exactly what Checkatrade stands for. Nothing feels better than a job done right.

03  /  Production

How It Was Made

Each episode was shot across a day and a half using four cameras: two principal cameras, a Steadicam, and a drone. The approach was observational documentary throughout. The production followed the action as it unfolded rather than constructing scenarios, with interviews picked up across the day to provide context and narrative connective tissue. Each shoot generated between 15 and 16 hours of rushes, which were then edited down to a 28 minute episode with a clear story arc and format beats running through it.

The Builds

Every job was a genuine build in a real home for a real family. The production did not know with certainty whether each job would finish in time. They overran. The celebrities stayed anyway, because they were building something that mattered. That authenticity cannot be manufactured and it is visible in every episode.

Rob Bent

Rob Bent had to do something almost nobody can do. He was actually building throughout the entire day. Sawing, drilling, fitting, finishing a real job in a real home, while simultaneously being funny, warm, quick on camera and keeping a completely clueless celebrity from losing their mind. That combination of genuine craft and genuine charisma is what made the series work. You cannot fake either of them.

Long Form By Design

Episodes run approximately 28 minutes. That was a deliberate creative commitment, not a default. Branded content typically retreats to short form out of anxiety about audience attention. Celebs With Tools trusted the format and the audience. The numbers confirmed that trust was well placed.

07  /  Why It Worked

The Outcome

Celebs With Tools showed what happens when a brand commits to putting entertainment genuinely first. Built around a real audience insight, cast for authenticity, and structured to feel native to how younger people actually watch content online, the series did not just reach a new audience. It gave Checkatrade something they had never had before: a reason to be watched.

A brand with a modest test target of 30,000 engagements got back 1.69 million. A brand aiming for 1 million views in a year got 4.61 million in a single month. From an audience that had never considered them before.
